cards.title: AI promised less work. I've never worked more

depth.text: someone says **AI made coding cheap**, but **juggling agents** has left them exhausted

The author's GitHub calendar shows **2,102 contributions by October 27**, more than any full year from 2021 to 2025. Several agents bring questions, plans and results, so **attention keeps shifting between problems**.

cards.camps: Some commenters say AI’s productivity gains mostly mean more work for employees, while others say it cuts mundane work or boosts output without increasing effort.
entities: The Reverse Centaur's Guide To Life After AI

cards.title: The US government is hiding secret court ruling about how it spies on Americans

depth.text: the Trump administration is hiding a **secret court ruling** as lawmakers debate **renewing the program**

The Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court objected to **search filters** that let intelligence analysts pull Americans’ messages from intercepted data without the approvals, written justifications, or records the law requires, but approved **another year of surveillance** anyway. cards.title: Python's experimental JIT to be removed

depth.text: Python's **experimental JIT** is set to leave the **main branch** after its maintainers withdrew the proposal

The **JIT** was added to CPython in **2024** for Python 3.13, but the council asked for a **standards-track proposal** covering support, maintenance and compatibility. Its authors said they lacked personal bandwidth and planned to make the reference implementation available; it's unclear whether they'll keep working on it.

cards.camps: Two camps: some see the JIT's end as a shame and blame bureaucracy or process; others say strict PEP review and concerns about maintenance, compatibility and security were justified.

cards.title: Wikipedia's Cleanup of AI-Generated Content

depth.text: volunteers are building new ways to spot and remove **AI-written material** from **Wikipedia**

In late 2025, Pangram flagged perhaps **20 percent** of new articles and drafts as AI-generated; in early 2026, it flagged **15 or 16 percent**. Lebleu says they don’t yet know whether the change came from recent policies or models getting more powerful. AI can find a real source but **get its content completely wrong**.

cards.title: Cross-request KV cache exposure in the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model (155 responses)

depth.text: a **bug** let some Workers AI replies include **other customers’ data** from earlier requests

Cloudflare counted **155 affected responses** between August 27 and September 9, all from prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. SGLang replaced rejected prompts with a **one-token placeholder**, but the decode node still read **stale cache pages** from earlier requests; Cloudflare fixed the pool configuration and patched the engine.

comments.text: This doesn't really have anything to do with GLM-5.3. This is what happens when you share models between users and don't do your bookkeeping properly, the actual model doesn't matter. What it shows is that there isn't enough isolation between the user sessions and that memory can overlap when that should never be possible. This is an SGLANG and a Cloudflare bug long before it is a Z.AI model bug…

I like this RCA a lot more than most. I appreciate the ownership and clear explanation of why their testing did not catch this bug. Also impressed with the speed to address the issue unplug the model and then pretty quick remediation, the speed to remediation matters less to me, but good to see they can act quickly on their platform to kill the serving of the model.

"We deployed GLM 5.3 with a 1,048,576-token context window, but the KV cache pool on our prefill GPUs only had room for 681,280 tokens. We were aware of this mismatch before launch. " Did they advertise it as 1,048,576 token when they only had room for 681,280 tokens?

What worries me is what was actually in those leaked prompts. This is a million-token context model, and people use that context to paste whole repos and configs, .env files included. So the realistic worst case isn't someone's chat text, it's someone's API keys. The write-up explains the root cause well, but doesn't say whether the customers whose prompts ended up in other people's responses…

cards.title: A Man from the Future: Why Johnny Can't Stop Abstracting

depth.text: John von Neumann kept finding the **simplest structure** underneath **messy problems**, from math to computers

He traces that habit from **defining numbers as sets** and treating set paradoxes like type errors, to showing matrix mechanics and wave mechanics were two forms of the same theory. His **stored-program design** put instructions and data in one memory, echoing his idea that a machine could reproduce itself by using a description as both instructions and data.

cards.title: Roblox downloaded 145GB models from us (including adult content) without asking

depth.text: a crawler claiming it was from **Roblox** downloaded creators’ models, including **adult content**

The sites say it took **1,027 files** from 712 projects—**145.5 GB** total—and 345 projects were adult content. They say the crawler ignored their robots.txt and creators’ licenses, but stress they **can't prove** Roblox ran it or that any files ended up in a model.

cards.title: The Exponential Time Hypothesis Is False [pdf]

depth.text: a paper claims the **Exponential Time Hypothesis** is false, but the result has **limits**

The comments describe a **subexponential-time** result for **3SAT**, but warn it does not extend to general NP problems: polynomial-time reductions can grow the input too much. One commenter also objects that a **lookup-based construction** relies on a machine with more states than the estimated physically distinguishable configurations of the observable universe.

cards.camps: Two camps: some call it an amazing result; others say the proof's lookup trick doesn't count as a meaningful fast algorithm.

comments.text: While this has no immediate bearing on P-vs-NP, it is interesting to note: - Early CS researchers like Donald Knuth entered CS in the days when regularly someone would come up with a surprising faster algorithm for some problem, and their intuitions were that most problems had faster algorithms than you'd expect. - Later generations of CS researchers, as all the easy algorithms were discovered…

This is an amazing and unexpected result. To be clear though, it does not imply that NP is subexponential: "Note that runtime bounds of the form 2^o(n) do not transfer under general polynomial-time reductions (2^n^o(1) would be needed for this), so our result does not imply that general NP problems
admit subexponential time algorithms." Edit: To explain more, it is guaranteed that you can reduce…

cards.title: Fixing Tool-Call Accuracy in vLLM

depth.text: someone got **tool calls** to follow their required format **every time** on the models they serve

Ubicloud first measured **Kimi K2.6** at **92%** tool-call accuracy, then saw the score fall to 91% after switching to vLLM's built-in version of constrained decoding, which wasn't enabled by default. Turning it on brought schema accuracy to 100% across served model versions. vLLM leaves it off by default because it has caused problems for some models and other serving features.

cards.camps: Two camps: some favor constrained decoding for reliable tool calls; others want it compared with retrying bad calls and question its effect on output quality.

comments.text: Constrained decoding has been in vLLM for a long time, and constrained tool call decoding has been in vLLM for a while, too. The blog post is rather confusing because until you understand the entire situation it appears to imply that they fixed vLLM (what the title implies) but really they just needed to configure it correctly. To be fair, the course of constrained tool calling configuration in…

Amusingly constrained decoding is the same approach we use to turn an AR model into a /v1/systemone endpoint (I worked on the vLLM feature). Tool calling is fraught with peril, especially because there's nothing that necessarily says that a models tools are fixed in place for the life of its run.
In some cases, tools are added mid-run to avoid a giant prefix miss and (at least last time I…

I wish they'd published something about the actual impact on model quality. Schema-constrained decoding changes the distribution the LLM will output. I'd be curious how a back-up-and-retry method for tool calls (which also doesn't pollute the context and also has 100% tool-call accuracy) would compare. In their example stats (23/25 success rate), it'd be +9% tokens used for the tool call attempt…

I'm one of the authors of this blog post. Figuring out how to integrate the LLM, the inference and serving engine, and the constrained decoding implementation such that you get the intended output and overall quality definitely requires careful engineering and testing. Please feel free to AMA. :)
